seo.best_title: How Did Ancient People Find a Partner?
seo.description_hook: How did ancient people find a partner before dating apps, phones or even writing? The answer involves Neanderthals, a marriage auction, and a Roman dating guide that got its author exiled.
paragraphs: In this animated history explainer we look at love and marriage in the ancient world: how Stone Age hunter-gatherers met people outside their small group, what ancient DNA tells us, and why every human outside Africa carries a little Neanderthal.

Then we visit Babylon's legendary marriage market, Egyptian love poems, Greek apple-throwing, the first engagement rings, Ovid's cheeky Roman dating advice, Chinese matchmakers and the red thread of fate, and the medieval poet who turned Valentine's Day into a romantic holiday.
Ancient dating, ancient marriage customs and everyday life in history, explained simply with stick figures and dry humour.

shorts.title: Your Ancestors Dated Neanderthals
shorts.description: Almost everyone outside Africa carries a little Neanderthal DNA. Here's why.
shorts.pinned: Did you know this before today?

shorts.title: Babylon's Strange Marriage Market
shorts.description: Herodotus said Babylon auctioned brides once a year. Historians aren't so sure.

shorts.title: A Roman Wrote a Dating Guide
shorts.description: Ovid's tips for the chariot races. Then the emperor exiled him.

shorts.title: The Ancient Chinese Red Thread of Fate
shorts.description: Matchmakers, fortune tellers and a god who ties your feet to your future partner.
shorts.pinned: Do you believe in the red thread?

shots.say: Today, finding a partner takes one thumb.
Swipe left. Swipe right. Hope for the best.
But for almost all of human history, there were no apps.
No phones. No bars. Often, no strangers at all.
shots.ai: a lonely stick figure in fur clothes sitting by a fire in a cave

shots.say: So how did ancient people actually find a partner?
Good luck finding someone new when everyone you know lives in your cave.
Here's a surprising clue. Your own DNA.

shots.title: COMING UP
shots.say: Today: Neanderthal romance, a marriage auction, and a banned dating guide.
Let's go back to the very beginning.
For most of prehistory, people lived in small groups.
A band of hunter-gatherers might be just a few dozen people.
Which creates an obvious problem. A tiny dating pool.
And many of those people are your cousins.

shots.title: THE SOLUTION
shots.say: The solution? Groups met up with other groups.
Seasonal gatherings, trade, feasts. Think of it as a giant party.
Basically a festival, minus the overpriced drinks.
Studies of modern hunter-gatherers back this up.
People moved between groups, and many bandmates weren't related at all.
shots.ai: two stick figures in fur clothes greeting each other between two stone age camps

shots.label: SUNGIR
shots.say: Ancient DNA tells the same story. Take Sungir, in Russia.
People were buried there about thirty-four thousand years ago.
Their DNA showed they weren't close relatives.
So even then, people looked for partners outside the family.
But here's the weird part.
Early humans also met a completely different kind of human.
shots.ai: a stick figure human awkwardly waving at a stockier stick figure Neanderthal in a forest, with a small heart between them

shots.say: Neanderthals. And yes, they had children together.
Most people outside Africa carry about one to two percent Neanderthal DNA.
So somewhere in your family tree, someone made a bold choice.
Then came farming, villages, and cities.
And marriage became serious business. Literally.

shots.label: BABYLON
shots.say: In Babylon, the Code of Hammurabi had rules about marriage.

shots.label: BRIDE-PRICE
shots.say: A groom's family often paid a bride-price to the bride's family.
Marriages came with contracts. Written on clay.

shots.label: MARRIAGE AUCTION
shots.say: Then there's the strangest story of all. A marriage auction.
shots.ai: a crowded ancient Babylonian market square with an auctioneer stick figure on a platform

shots.say: The Greek historian Herodotus said it happened once a year.

shots.title: HERODOTUS' VERSION
shots.say: Rich men bid on brides. The money paid dowries for the women nobody bid on.
But most historians doubt it happened like that, if at all.
Herodotus loved a good story. Fact-checking, less so.

shots.label: EGYPT
shots.say: Meanwhile, in Egypt, people were writing love poems.
Love songs on papyrus survive from over three thousand years ago.
And honestly? Some of them are really sweet.
Lovers waiting by the river. Hearts racing. Sleepless nights.
shots.ai: two stick figures in white robes sitting by the Nile at sunset with a small heart above them

shots.say: One confusing detail. Lovers called each other brother and sister.
Relax. It was just a pet name. Like calling someone babe.
And marriage? Often it just meant moving into the same house.
shots.ai: a happy stick figure carrying belongings into a small mud brick house in ancient Egypt

shots.say: No big ceremony required. Very low-budget wedding.
Now, Rome. Rich Roman marriages were mostly arranged by families.
Love was nice, but money and family alliances came first.

shots.label: OVID
shots.say: But around 2 AD, a poet named Ovid wrote a dating guide.
shots.ai: a smug stick figure in a toga holding a scroll

shots.title: OVID'S TIPS
shots.say: His advice? Go to the chariot races. Sit close. Make small talk.
If dust lands on her dress, brush it off. Even if there's no dust.
Two thousand years later, people still try this move.

shots.label: AUGUSTUS
shots.say: Emperor Augustus was not a fan. He was promoting family values.
shots.ai: an angry stick figure emperor with a crown and crossed arms

shots.label: BLACK SEA
shots.say: In 8 AD, Ovid was exiled to the edge of the Black Sea.
He blamed a poem and a mistake. Historians still argue about it.
Before Rome, the Greeks had a very strange flirting move.
They threw an apple at the person they liked.
shots.ai: a stick figure in a toga tossing an apple to a surprised stick figure in a Greek olive grove

shots.say: Catching it meant yes. Getting hit in the face meant, well, ouch.

shots.label: LOVE APPLE
shots.say: There's even an old Greek poem built around this apple toss.
The Romans gave us something more lasting. The engagement ring.

shots.label: IRON RING
shots.say: Early Roman betrothal rings were often plain iron.
shots.ai: a happy stick figure in a toga offering a small plain iron ring

shots.say: Worn on the fourth finger of the left hand.

shots.title: THE ROMAN THEORY
shots.say: A Roman writer said a nerve ran from that finger straight to the heart.
Anatomy says no. But the tradition stuck anyway.
And when charm didn't work, some people tried magic.

shots.label: LOVE SPELLS
shots.say: Greek and Egyptian spell books include love charms.
Potions, chants, little figures, and spells written on lead.
shots.ai: a nervous stick figure holding a potion bottle by a fire under the moon

shots.say: Some of these spells were honestly a bit creepy.
Spoiler: there's no evidence any of them worked.

shots.label: CHINA
shots.say: In ancient China, you usually didn't pick your partner at all.
A matchmaker did. Families hired one to find a good match.
shots.ai: a smug stick figure matchmaker in a robe talking to a nervous stick figure family in an ancient Chinese village

shots.title: THE MATCH
shots.say: Birth dates were checked for luck. Gifts went back and forth.
Sometimes the couple barely met before the wedding.
But there's also a lovely legend. The red thread of fate.

shots.label: OLD MAN UNDER THE MOON
shots.say: The old man under the moon ties a red thread between future partners.
shots.ai: an old stick figure sitting under a big moon holding a long red thread

shots.say: However far apart, the thread will bring them together.
In medieval Europe, families and the church shaped most marriages.
But young people still met at markets, church, and village festivals.
And one poet changed romance forever.

shots.label: CHAUCER
shots.say: Around 1382, Geoffrey Chaucer wrote about birds choosing mates on Valentine's Day.
shots.ai: a stick figure poet in a robe writing outdoors while birds pair up around him

shots.say: It's the oldest known link between Valentine's Day and romance.
So if you hate Valentine's Day, you know who to blame.

shots.title: HOW WE MET
shots.say: From festivals, to contracts, to chariot races, to phones.
Honestly? The basics haven't changed much.

shots.title: STILL TRUE
shots.say: Meet new people. Try to be charming. Hope it works.
But finding a partner was only half the story.
What happened when an ancient marriage went wrong?
Ancient divorce is next. The Egyptians were surprisingly modern.
